passage_text: Researchers at the University of Northbridge examined the impact of caffeine on working‑memory performance in healthy adults. A double‑blind, randomized crossover design was employed, with 40 participants (age 20–35, 22 females) receiving either a 200‑mg caffeine dose or a placebo on separate test days. Each session began with a 30‑minute acclimation period, followed by a 20‑item N‑back task. Reaction times (RT) and accuracy were recorded. The study aimed to determine whether caffeine could enhance cognitive speed and whether any benefits were moderated by baseline sleep quality. Participants also completed a sleep diary the week prior to each session. The researchers hypothesized that caffeine would reduce mean RT and increase accuracy, particularly in participants reporting poor sleep. The data are summarized in Table 1 below.
stem: According to Table 1, what is the mean reaction time (RT) for participants who received the caffeine dose?
explanation: The table lists the mean RT for the caffeine condition as 520 ms.
trap: The numbers for the caffeine + poor sleep condition (530 ms) might tempt readers to choose that value.

stem: Which experimental design element best controls for individual differences in baseline cognitive ability?
explanation: A randomized crossover design allows each participant to serve as their own control, thereby minimizing variability due to baseline cognitive differences.
trap: Some may incorrectly assume the placebo control is the primary control for individual differences.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: Caffeine reduces mean RT relative to placebo.
options.B: Participants with poor sleep experience a greater RT benefit from caffeine.
options.C: The study used a double‑blind design.
options.D: Caffeine increases accuracy in the N‑back task.

explanation: The passage reports only reaction times; accuracy data are not provided, so the claim about increased accuracy is unsupported.
trap: Readers may assume accuracy was measured because RT was, leading to an incorrect choice.

passage_text: Researchers at the University of Northbridge examined the impact of caffeine on working‑memory performance in healthy adults. A double‑blind, randomized crossover design was employed, with 40 participants (age 20–35, 22 females) receiving either a 200‑mg caffeine dose or a placebo on separate test days. Each session began with a 30‑minute acclimation period, followed by a 20‑item N‑back task. Reaction times (RT) and accuracy were recorded. The study aimed to determine whether caffeine could enhance cognitive speed and whether any benefits were moderated by baseline sleep quality. Participants also completed a sleep diary the week prior to each session. The researchers hypothesized that caffeine would reduce mean RT and increase accuracy, particularly in participants reporting poor sleep. The data are summarized in Table 1 below.
stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: Caffeine (200 mg) lowered mean reaction time by about 70 ms relative to placebo in this sample.
options.B: Caffeine is safe for long-term daily use.
options.C: Caffeine lowers reaction time only in participants with poor sleep.
options.D: Caffeine increased N-back accuracy most in poor sleepers.

explanation: Correct: Mean RT was 520 ms with caffeine and 590 ms with placebo, a 70 ms difference. Why the others are wrong: B) the study tested a single dose on separate days and says nothing about long-term safety. C) caffeine also lowered RT in the full sample (520 vs 590 ms), not only in poor sleepers. D) Table 1 reports no accuracy data.
trap: Extending a single-dose, short-term reaction-time result to long-term safety or to subgroup effects the table does not show.
